title: Technology momentum offsets part of the war drag while growth, inflation, and fiscal room remain uneven across economies
source_unit: International Monetary Fund, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
geography: Global economy with advanced, emerging-market, developing, energy-importing, and technology-integrated economy comparisons

unevenness.value: growth is holding up but remains uneven across countries

offsetting_forces.value: AI-driven demand is lifting economies integrated into global technology value chains while war weighs on energy importers and vulnerable economies

observations.method: IMF World Economic Outlook update using macroeconomic projections, country group comparisons, and scenario/risk analysis.
observations.uncertainty: These are forecasts, not realized outcomes; conflict, energy prices, financial conditions, trade, technology investment, and policy responses can change the path.
observations.subgroup: Energy-importing economies, vulnerable economies, technology-integrated economies, workers, firms, consumers, and public finance authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Resilient global growth can coexist with severe regional stress; headline expansion does not imply equal household purchasing room or job quality.

denominator.unit: global conflict, energy, and macroeconomic risk frame

war_drag.value: the war shock weighs on energy importers and vulnerable economies

downside_risks.value: renewed conflict, financial-market repricing, and further geopolitical strains remain downside risks

exposure_difference.value: the same geopolitical shock transmits differently depending on energy dependence, fiscal space, market access, and economic structure

observations.method: IMF scenario and risk analysis linking geopolitical developments to energy, finance, trade, and growth channels.
observations.uncertainty: The update does not estimate each household's energy bill, firm loss, or political response; transmission depends on policy, buffers, substitution, and market conditions.
observations.subgroup: Energy importers, low-income economies, exposed firms, consumers facing higher prices, workers in affected sectors, and governments with limited buffers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Diversified supply, energy efficiency, fiscal support, financial regulation, and trade adjustment can reduce—but not eliminate—shock transmission.

observations.period: 2026; AI-driven demand and technology value chains

denominator.unit: technology investment, demand, and global value-chain frame

technology_tailwind.value: AI-driven demand is supporting economies integrated into global technology value chains

distributional_exposure.value: technology-linked gains are concentrated in economies and sectors with relevant infrastructure, capital, skills, and market integration

risk_balance.value: technology momentum offsets part of the war drag but does not remove downside risks from repricing or renewed conflict

observations.method: IMF macroeconomic outlook combining technology-demand assumptions with country and sector exposure analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The update does not provide a causal estimate of AI productivity, employment, or household welfare; value-chain exposure and technology adoption remain heterogeneous.
observations.subgroup: Technology-integrated economies, firms, skilled and less-skilled workers, capital owners, suppliers, and places with weak digital infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technology diffusion can broaden productivity and service access if infrastructure, skills, competition, and public capacity prevent gains from becoming concentrated.

observations.period: 2026; inflation, fiscal space, and policy response

denominator.unit: global disinflation, fiscal, and macro-policy frame

policy_priorities.value: policymakers should preserve price stability, rebuild fiscal space, and strengthen adaptability

household_channel.value: persistent price pressure can compress household purchasing room and increase political pressure even when output growth remains positive

institutional_tradeoff.value: fiscal rebuilding, price stability, resilience investment, and support for exposed groups can pull policy in different directions

observations.method: IMF inflation outlook and macro-policy synthesis across monetary, fiscal, and structural adaptation channels.
observations.uncertainty: The report-level recommendation does not identify the optimal policy mix for any one country or prove a direct effect on public trust, consumption, or political behavior.
observations.subgroup: Households facing price pressure, borrowers, savers, workers, vulnerable groups, taxpayers, central banks, and finance ministries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credible policy, targeted support, stronger competition, and supply-side adaptation can reduce the social cost of disinflation without treating aggregate stability as sufficient.

related_sources.claim: The IMF World Economic Outlook series provides the broader forecast and historical update context.
The IMF Global Financial Stability Report provides complementary financial-repricing and market-risk analysis.

boundary: This record adds a global macro route across war, energy, technology demand, growth, inflation, fiscal space, and unequal exposure. It uses IMF forecasts and report-level risk synthesis, not respondent-level data, household price diaries, firm microdata, causal AI productivity estimates, or proof that aggregate growth improves welfare evenly.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IMF July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update page reviewed for global growth projections, war and energy-importer exposure, AI-driven technology-value-chain demand, stalled disinflation, downside risks, and policy priorities.
